name: English Gypsy, old
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Smart, Bath C. & Crofton, Henry Thomas. 1875. The Dialect of the English Gypsies. 2nd ed., revised and greatly enlarged. London: Asher & Co.
catalog_locator: Grammar, section 'ACCENT', pp. 7-8; also Noun, nominative plural (p. ~16) and Verb, 1st pers. plural (pp. 38-39); archive.org item dialectofenglish00smaruoft d…
catalog_quote: ACCENT. In the Turkish dialect, the accent is usually on the last syllable; but if the word is inflected, or liable to inflection, the accent is placed on the first syllable of the inflection, e.g., Bar-6, great. Gen. bar-^skoro; pi. bar-e. Beshdva, I sit; besh-ela, He sits. Relics of this system are found in the old dialect of this country, e.g., BaurS, great; pi., bmird. Bcsh-ova, I sit; besh-eia, He sits. Words too ending in -engro, -eskro, (elsewhere shown to be inflections,) invariably take the accent on the first syllable of those terminations, in both the old and new dialects. In the new dialect, dissyllables and trisyllables take an accent on the first syllable, and words of four or five syllables take an accent on the first and third, e.g., Bauro, great Beshto, saddle Bengalo, diabolic Brisheuo, rainy B<^romMgro, sailor Sdvlohdloben, oath Boshofn^iigro, fiddler Tdssermengri…

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim in both the scanned text we hold and the PDF page scan we hold (book pp. 7-8), plus the two supporting locators (nom. pl. -é, 1pl -ás). The deciding source is a 19th-century grammar sketch, but it is the primary first-hand record of an extinct variety; Glottolog 5.3's relabelling of angl1239 as 'Archaic Angloromani' under British Romani matches the record's 'English Gypsy, old' identity, so no identity problem. sources.note: Only modern linguistic synthesis of the extinct inflected English Romani ('old dialect') that our morphological coding describes; would say whether the stem-final / inflection-initial accent of Smart & Crofton is treated as the system of British Romani or as relics within a variety already shifted to English-type initial stress (which would bear on classification morphological vs initial).

tone.says: Record + open review only: ch. 3 (pp. 57-94) gives a structural and dialectological profile of British/Welsh Romani within the Northern dialect group, revising Matras 2002; its phonology diagnostics very likely include the conservative word-level (final/grammatical) stress that Matras 2002 §4.2.6 attributes to Welsh Romani after Sampson 1926: 23-8; no lexical tone is expected to be reported (Romani is described throughout this literature as a stress language). Content unseen.
